NOTICE OF PENDENCY OF ACTION (LIS PENDENS), EXPUNGEMENT, AND WITHDRAWAL — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 742 Oak St., Fresno, CA 93721 (APN 123-456-789) · Fresno

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes what California law provides about a notice of pendency of action — the recorded document commonly called a lis pendens — as it may bear on the real property at 742 Oak St., Fresno, CA 93721 (APN 123-456-789) in Fresno County and on the interest of Jordan Lee. It states what Title 4.5 of Part 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure (sections 405 through 405.61) provides about who may record such a notice, what a “real property claim” is, how the notice must be signed, mailed, recorded, and filed with the court, what effect recording has on later purchasers and encumbrancers, how a court may expunge the notice and who carries the burden of proof, when an undertaking may be required, how an expungement order is reviewed, when attorney's fees are awarded on a motion, and what happens to the notice's effect when it is withdrawn or expunged. It also states what Civil Code section 47 provides about when a recorded lis pendens is a privileged publication. It does not determine whether any notice, pleading, claim, or motion concerning 742 Oak St., Fresno, CA 93721 (APN 123-456-789) is valid, and it does not tell Jordan Lee what to do about any dispute.

WHAT A NOTICE OF PENDENCY OF ACTION IS, WHO MAY RECORD ONE, AND WHICH COURTS' ACTIONS IT COVERS
California's lis pendens scheme is Title 4.5 of Part 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, sections 405 through 405.61, repealed and re-added by Statutes 1992, chapter 883. Section 405.2 defines the central document: a "notice of pendency of action" or "notice" means a notice of the pendency of an action in which a real property claim is alleged. Section 405.1 defines the person who records it: a "claimant" is a party to an action who asserts a real property claim and records a notice of the pendency of the action. Section 405.20 states who may record and where: a party to an action who asserts a real property claim may record a notice of pendency of action in which that real property claim is alleged, the notice may be recorded in the office of the recorder of each county in which all or part of the real property is situated, and the notice must contain the names of all parties to the action and a description of the property affected by the action. The California Supreme Court has described the document's function in one sentence: a lis pendens is a recorded document giving constructive notice that an action has been filed affecting title or right to possession of the real property described in the notice. Section 405.5 extends the title beyond the state courts: it applies to an action pending in any United States District Court in the same manner that it applies to an action pending in the courts of this state. Section 405.8 preserves other remedies, providing that nothing in the title precludes any party from seeking an attachment, injunction, or other relief in connection with a real property claim or the expungement of a notice of pending action.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF A "REAL PROPERTY CLAIM"
Everything in the scheme turns on whether the pleading contains a "real property claim." Section 405.4 defines the term as the cause or causes of action in a pleading which would, if meritorious, affect (a) title to, or the right to possession of, specific real property or (b) the use of an easement identified in the pleading, other than an easement obtained pursuant to statute by any regulated public utility. Two features of that definition recur in the cases. First, the test looks to the cause of action as pled and asks what effect it would have if it succeeded, not to the plaintiff's motive: in Kirkeby v. Superior Court the California Supreme Court held that a fraudulent conveyance cause of action seeking to void a transfer of real property is a real property claim, reasoning that by definition the voiding of a transfer of real property will affect title to or possession of real property, and that it could not ignore the plain language of the statute, which clearly establishes that fraudulent conveyance claims may support a lis pendens where the plaintiff seeks to void a fraudulent transfer. Second, the easement prong of subdivision (b) reaches both sides of an easement dispute: in Park 100 Investment Group II, LLC v. Ryan the Court of Appeal held it is proper to record a notice of pendency of action on a dominant tenement when the litigation is an easement dispute — that is, on the parcel benefited by the claimed easement, not only on the parcel burdened by it.

WHO MAY SIGN THE NOTICE, AND THE TWO STATUTORY EXCEPTIONS
Section 405.21 makes the signature on the notice a recording prerequisite. An attorney of record in the action may sign a notice of pendency of action. Alternatively, a judge of the court in which an action that includes a real property claim is pending may, upon request of a party, approve a notice of pendency of action. The section then states the negative rule: a notice of pendency of action shall not be recorded unless (a) it has been signed by the attorney of record, (b) it is signed by a party acting in propria persona and approved by a judge as provided in the section, or (c) the action is subject to section 405.6. A self-represented party therefore proceeds under the second route, judicial approval, rather than by signing alone. Two categories of action sit outside the ordinary Chapter 2 recording and service machinery. Section 405.6 provides that in an action by a public agency in eminent domain pursuant to Title 7 (commencing with Section 1230.010) of Part 3, the issuance, service, and recordation of a notice of pendency of action is governed by Section 1250.150 and is not subject to Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 405.20). Section 405.7 imposes an affirmative duty in a different setting: whenever an action is commenced to declare a building uninhabitable, the plaintiff public agency, at the time of filing the complaint, must record in the office of the recorder of the county in which the building is situated a notice of the pendency of the action, containing the names of the parties and a description of the real property upon which the building affected by the action is situated.

MAILING BEFORE RECORDING, FILING WITH THE COURT AFTER, AND THE CONSEQUENCE OF FAILING EITHER
Section 405.22 sequences three steps around the act of recording. Before recording, the claimant must cause a copy of the notice to be mailed, by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested, to all known addresses of the parties to whom the real property claim is adverse and to all owners of record of the real property affected by the real property claim as shown by the latest county assessment roll. If there is no known address for service on an adverse party or owner, then as to that party or owner a declaration under penalty of perjury to that effect may be recorded instead of the proof of service, and service on that party or owner is not required. Immediately following recordation, a copy of the notice must also be filed with the court in which the action is pending, and service must also be made immediately and in the same manner upon each adverse party later joined in the action. Section 405.23 attaches a consequence to those requirements: any notice of pendency of action is void and invalid as to any adverse party or owner of record unless the requirements of section 405.22 are met for that party or owner and a proof of service in the form and content specified in section 1013a has been recorded with the notice of pendency of action. The voiding operates party by party — the section speaks of invalidity "as to any adverse party or owner of record" for whom the requirements were not met.

THE EFFECT OF RECORDING: CONSTRUCTIVE NOTICE TO LATER TRANSFEREES AND RELATION BACK
Section 405.24 states the two consequences that give a recorded notice its practical force. First, from the time of recording the notice, a purchaser, encumbrancer, or other transferee of the real property described in the notice is deemed to have constructive notice of the pendency of the noticed action as it relates to the real property, and only of its pendency against parties not fictitiously named. Second, the rights and interest of the claimant in the property, as ultimately determined in the pending noticed action, relate back to the date of the recording of the notice. The effect is not a lien and not an injunction: the property may still be transferred or encumbered, but a transferee who takes after recording takes subject to whatever the claimant is ultimately determined to have, measured from the recording date rather than from the date of judgment. The statute's fictitious-name limitation means that constructive notice runs only as to the pendency of the action against parties who are named, not against parties sued under fictitious names.

THE MOTION TO EXPUNGE: WHO MAY BRING IT, WHERE, AND WHO BEARS THE BURDEN
Section 405.30 sets the procedural frame for removing a recorded notice. At any time after a notice of pendency of action has been recorded, any party, or any nonparty with an interest in the real property affected by it, may apply to the court in which the action is pending to expunge the notice; a person who is not a party must obtain leave to intervene from the court at or before the time the party brings the motion. Evidence or declarations may be filed with the motion, the court may permit evidence to be received in the form of oral testimony, and it may make any orders it deems just to provide for discovery by any party affected by the motion. The section then allocates the burden in a way that reverses the ordinary rule for motions: the claimant — the party who recorded the notice — has the burden of proof under sections 405.31 and 405.32. The California Supreme Court stated the point directly in Kirkeby: unlike most other motions, when a motion to expunge is brought, the burden is on the party opposing the motion to show the existence of a real property claim. The forum is also fixed by the statute's words. In The Formula Inc. v. Superior Court, the Court of Appeal read "the court in which the action is pending" literally and held that a California court could not expunge, under section 405.30, a notice of litigation pending in the courts of another state, because the California lis pendens statutes do not reach such a notice at all.

GROUND ONE FOR EXPUNGEMENT: THE PLEADING DOES NOT CONTAIN A REAL PROPERTY CLAIM
Section 405.31 states the first ground for expungement and makes it mandatory: in proceedings under the chapter, the court shall order the notice expunged if the court finds that the pleading on which the notice is based does not contain a real property claim. The same section forbids softening that result with security: the court shall not order an undertaking to be given as a condition of expunging the notice where the court finds the pleading does not contain a real property claim. The California Supreme Court has described the inquiry as a limited, demurrer-like one directed at the pleading rather than at the evidence or at the claimant's motives: review of an expungement order under section 405.31 is limited to whether a real property claim has been properly pled by the claimant. In Kirkeby, the property owners argued that a court must look past the pleadings to determine the purpose of the party maintaining the notice. The Supreme Court rejected that argument, holding that it failed based on the plain language of the applicable statute and that nowhere in the language of section 405.31, or in its legislative history, is the court directed to conduct such an examination during its demurrer-like analysis.

GROUND TWO FOR EXPUNGEMENT: THE CLAIMANT HAS NOT ESTABLISHED PROBABLE VALIDITY
Section 405.32 states a second, evidentiary ground, also mandatory. In proceedings under the chapter, the court shall order that the notice be expunged if the court finds that the claimant has not established by a preponderance of the evidence the probable validity of the real property claim; and the court shall not order an undertaking to be given as a condition of expunging the notice if it finds the claimant has not established that probable validity. Section 405.3 supplies the measure: "probable validity," with respect to a real property claim, means that it is more likely than not that the claimant will obtain a judgment against the defendant on the claim. Read with section 405.30, which places the burden of proof under sections 405.31 and 405.32 on the claimant, the result is that a claimant faced with a motion to expunge must affirmatively carry a merits showing rather than simply rest on the pleading. The Court of Appeal has described the historical reason for that structure: because of a history of abuse of the lis pendens system by third party claimants, the statutes were amended to counterbalance the protection afforded third party litigants with new protections for the interests of property owners and prospective purchasers, and those amendments have created a balance in which the interests of third party litigant claimants, property owners, and prospective purchasers are protected by a somewhat complicated procedural scheme. The California Supreme Court has noted the pressure that makes the balance necessary: while the lis pendens statute was designed to give notice to third parties and not to aid plaintiffs in pursuing claims, the practical effect of a recorded lis pendens is to render a defendant's property unmarketable and unsuitable as security for a loan.

Section 405.4 defines the term as the cause or causes of action in a pleading which would, if meritorious, affect (a) title to, or the right to possession of, specific real property or (b) the use of an easement identified in the pleading, other than an easement obtained pursuant to statute by any regulated public utility. Section 405.39 channels review away from appeal: no order or other action of the court under the chapter is appealable, and any party aggrieved by an order made on a motion under the chapter may petition the proper reviewing court to review the order by writ of mandate. The petition must be filed and served within 20 days of service of written notice of the order by the court or any party, and the court which issued the order may, within the initial 20-day period, extend it for one additional period not to exceed 10 days. Section 405.35 keeps the order off the record in the meantime: no order expunging a notice of pendency of action is effective, or recordable in the office of any county recorder, until the time for filing a writ petition under section 405.39 has expired, and if a petition is timely filed the order remains ineffective and unrecordable until the proceeding commenced by the petition is finally adjudicated. That section also states that it imposes no duty on the county recorder to determine whether its requirements or those of any expungement order have been met. Section 405.36 closes the door on a second notice: once a notice of pending action has been expunged, the claimant may not record another notice of pending action as to the affected property without leave of the court in which the action is pending. The Court of Appeal has summarized the last two points together: when a lis pendens has been expunged, the claimant may record another notice of pendency of action only with leave of court, and an order expunging a lis pendens is not appealable but must be challenged by petition for writ of mandate.

expectedJSON.body: A claimant need not wait for a motion. Section 405.50 provides that at any time after a notice of pendency of an action has been recorded pursuant to the title or other law, the notice may be withdrawn by recording, in the office of the recorder in which the notice of pendency was recorded, a notice of withdrawal executed by the party who recorded the notice of pendency of action or by that party's successor in interest, and the notice of withdrawal must be acknowledged. Two sections then wipe out the recorded notice's informational effect. Under section 405.60, upon withdrawal under section 405.50 or upon recordation of a certified copy of an order expunging the notice, neither the notice nor any information derived from it — before the recording of a certified copy of the judgment or decree issued in the action — constitutes actual or constructive notice of any of the matters contained, claimed, alleged, or contended in it, or of any matters related to the action, or creates a duty of inquiry in any person thereafter dealing with the affected property. Section 405.61 goes further and reaches actual knowledge: after such a withdrawal or expungement, no person except a nonfictitious party to the action at the time of recording of the notice of withdrawal or order, who thereafter becomes a purchaser, transferee, mortgagee, or other encumbrancer for a valuable consideration by a conveyance recorded before a certified copy of the judgment or decree is recorded, is deemed to have actual knowledge of the action or its subject matter, irrespective of whether that person possessed actual knowledge and irrespective of when or how the knowledge was obtained. The Legislature stated its aim in the section itself: it is the intent of the Legislature that the section provide for the absolute and complete free transferability of real property after the expungement or withdrawal of a notice of pendency of action.

expectedJSON.body: Recording a notice of pendency of action is also a publication about the property, which is why the Civil Code privilege statute addresses it by name. Civil Code section 47, subdivision (b), makes a publication in a judicial proceeding privileged, subject to listed exceptions; paragraph (4) of those exceptions provides that a recorded lis pendens is not a privileged publication unless it identifies an action previously filed with a court of competent jurisdiction which affects the title or right of possession of real property, as authorized or required by law. The privilege therefore turns on the same question as expungement: whether the identified action is one affecting title or the right of possession. The Court of Appeal applied that provision in Park 100 Investment Group II, LLC v. Ryan, stating that section 47, subdivision (b)(4), provided an absolute privilege to the filing of the lis pendens in that case, and concluding that because the lis pendens alleged a real property claim and was privileged, and because the opposing owner had made no argument that the lis pendens lacked merit for other reasons, recordation of the lis pendens could not be the basis for intentional interference with prospective economic advantage or slander of title causes of action, even if the recording party acted with malice.
